subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Kitchen Observations — What Makes Things Work?
periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Discuss what makes things in a kitchen move, shine, make a sound, or get warm and cold (p. 115)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of a kitchen scene (p. 115)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to close their eyes and picture a busy kitchen at home — what is moving, what is glowing, what sounds can they hear, what feels warm. Students share their images aloud, building a class word-cloud on the board: move, shine, sound, warm, change.

Students open Textbook p. 115 and study the kitchen illustration. In pairs they make a quick list of all the activities they can spot — food cooking on a stove, a fan turning, a light glowing, a pressure-cooker whistling — and say what each activity needs to happen.

Pairs share their lists. The teacher guides a whole-class discussion linking each activity to the idea that something must be available to make it happen — that 'something' is what the chapter calls energy. Students copy a one-sentence class definition into their notebooks.

Students respond individually in their notebooks to the question from Textbook p. 115: 'What makes these things move, shine, make a sound, or get warm and cold?' — written in their own words. Two or three responses are shared aloud to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify observable phenomena in everyday environments and connect each to a common underlying cause.
periods.section_context: Kitchen activities — cooking, fan movement, lighting, pressure-cooker sound, warmth; idea of energy as the cause of change.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'If you switched off all sources of energy in the kitchen, what would stop happening first?' to push students beyond listing toward reasoning. Invite children from different home settings — those who cook on wood fires or kerosene stoves, not just gas or electric — to share, so the discussion stays locally grounded.

periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Blow up a balloon, hold it, release it, and observe what happens (p. 116)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly revisits the class definition of energy noted during earlier work on kitchen observations, then poses the inquiry question: 'Can we feel stored energy being released?' Students predict what will happen when a blown-up balloon is released.

In pairs, students follow the instructions on Textbook p. 116: blow the balloon until it is full, hold it tightly, then release the mouth and observe. They record three things they notice — what the balloon does, what they feel against their hand, and any sound produced.

Pairs share their observations. The teacher facilitates comparison: some balloons flew far, some spun, some made noise. Students discuss what was stored in the balloon and what form it took on release, arriving at the idea of energy changing from a stored form into movement and sound.
Students write a two-sentence conclusion in their notebooks: what the balloon experiment showed about energy and how it connects to the class definition from the previous discussion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple inquiry, record observations, and draw a conclusion about energy changing from one form to another.
periods.section_context: Balloon blown up and released — stored energy converted to movement and sound (kinetic energy).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'What would you need to do to make the balloon go even further?' to extend reasoning toward the idea that more stored energy produces more effect. Let groups try releasing at different angles if time allows, keeping the exploration unhurried.

periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Observe what happens when a balloon releases air (p. 116)
materials: Rubber bands of different thicknesses (two or three per group)
Empty box or open container (shoebox or similar)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'When you pluck a rubber band stretched over a box, what do you expect to happen?' Students predict in one sentence. The class agrees on what they will test: does a tighter or thicker rubber band make a higher or lower sound?

Groups stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses across an open box to create a simple guitar. They pluck each band and listen carefully, then vary the tension by pressing a finger partway along the band and plucking again. Students record in a simple two-column table: band type or tension change → sound change observed.

Groups share findings. The teacher draws out the connection: plucking puts energy into the band, the band vibrates, the vibration travels through air as sound. Students connect this to the earlier balloon activity — both show energy changing form, here from the movement of a finger into sound energy.
Students write a one-sentence summary connecting the rubber-band guitar to the concept of energy changing form, to be kept alongside the balloon conclusion in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate through a hands-on investigation that mechanical action transfers energy and produces a detectable change in another form.
periods.section_context: Rubber bands of different thicknesses stretched over a box — plucking produces sound; varying tension or thickness changes pitch; sound energy from kinetic energy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Which part of the guitar carries the energy to your ear?' to surface the idea of vibration as the carrier. Encourage students to place a finger lightly on the vibrating band to feel, not just hear, the energy.

periods.activity_title: Diyas and Fuels — What Keeps a Flame Burning?
periods.textbook_anchor: Sources of Energy — Light two diyas, one with oil and one without, and observe which burns longer and what acts as fuel (p. 120)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the question: 'Food gives us energy to move — what gives a flame its energy?' Students discuss in pairs where the energy for a cooking fire might come from, recording their prediction on a slip of paper.

Following the instructions on Textbook p. 120, the teacher sets up two diyas at the front: Diya 1 has a dry cotton wick, Diya 2 has a wick soaked in oil. The teacher lights both under the class's observation. Students record in a table: what each diya looks like at the start, what happens as time passes, and which burns longer.

The class discusses their observations. The teacher draws out the two questions from the textbook task: which diya burns longer and why, and what is acting as the fuel. Students connect oil to other fuels discussed in the section — petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood, coal — as substances that release energy when they burn.

Students answer the two textbook questions from Textbook p. 120 in writing in their notebooks, then respond to the teacher's prompt: 'What problems could burning too much wood or coal cause?' — linking to the pollution discussion in the section.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a controlled comparison, record what changes and what stays the same, and identify the factor responsible for the observed difference.
periods.section_context: Two diyas — one dry wick, one oil-soaked wick; oil as fuel; comparison of burning duration; fuels including petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood, coal; pollution from burning wood or coal.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students about the kinds of fuel their own families use for cooking — wood, gas, kerosene, or electricity — and whether the fuel choice differs by season or place. If students mention traditional practices like cooking on a chulha or storing firewood, invite them to share how their family manages fuel use across the year.

periods.activity_title: Cattle, Cold Climates, and Heat from Living Things
periods.textbook_anchor: Sources of Energy — Discuss what kind of fuel is used at home for cooking (p. 120)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration or photograph of traditional multi-floor house layout with cattle on ground floor (if present in chapter)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Besides food and fuel, can you think of anything living that gives off heat?' Students share ideas — animals, human bodies, even compost heaps. The class is invited to think about whether people have ever used that living warmth deliberately.

Students read or listen to the section describing how in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh, families traditionally keep cattle on the ground floor of their homes so the animals' body heat rises and warms the family living above. Students discuss in small groups: why would this be especially important in those regions? What does it replace? How does it reduce the need for firewood or electricity?

Groups share their reasoning with the class. The teacher connects the discussion to food as energy source — animals eat food, their bodies release heat, and that heat becomes useful energy for the family. Students note how this is a clever, low-cost way of using a natural energy source that already exists in the household.

Students respond in their notebooks to the writing task from Textbook p. 119: 'How is food cooked in your house?' — extending their answer to name the energy source involved and compare it to the cattle-heat practice discussed in class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a natural energy source and a traditional cultural practice that harnesses it.
periods.section_context: Cattle kept on ground floor in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh to warm the family above; animal body heat as energy source; food as fuel for humans and animals; reduction of firewood and electricity use.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Could a similar idea work in your own region, or would it need to be different? Why?' to encourage students to reason about how geography shapes energy practices. Invite students whose families keep animals to describe where those animals sleep and whether the family notices any warmth from them.

periods.activity_title: Electricity at Home — Devices, Uses, and Safety
periods.textbook_anchor: Electricity — Walk around the home or classroom, identify five things that run on electricity, and fill in a table of device, what it does, and what it requires (p. 121)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram listing energy outputs: light, sound, heat, movement, cooling

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'What would you switch off first if you wanted to save electricity tonight?' Students name devices, and the teacher lists them on the board. Together the class notices that different devices produce different kinds of output — light, sound, heat, movement, cooling.

Students follow the activity on Textbook p. 121: they move quietly around the classroom observing every electrical device they can find (lights, fan, any plug points, switches) and add devices they know from home. They fill in the table in their notebooks — device name, what it does, and what kind of output it requires.

Students share their tables. The class builds a combined list on the board. The teacher introduces the energy-efficiency idea from the 'Do you know?' box — that an LED bulb gives the same light as an older bulb while using far less electricity — and connects this to the traditional Indian design of houses with small windows and thick walls as passive cooling.

The teacher leads a focused discussion on electrical safety rules from the section — not touching bare wires, staying away from fallen poles, not inserting objects into sockets. Students write three safety rules in their own words as the closing activity.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe and classify devices in their environment by the type of energy output they produce.
periods.section_context: Electrical devices in home and classroom — fan, light, radio, heater, refrigerator; energy outputs: light, sound, heat, movement, cooling; LED bulbs as energy-efficient option; traditional Indian house design with small windows and thick walls; electrical safety rules.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'If your village or neighbourhood has power cuts often, which device do people miss most and why?' to connect the observation task to lived experience. Students in areas with irregular electricity may have richer insights about which devices are most essential.

periods.activity_title: Pinwheel in the Wind — Making a Wind Energy Model
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Make a paper pinwheel and observe what happens when it is held in the wind or when running (p. 123)
materials: Square sheets of paper (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of pinwheel construction steps (p. 123)

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows a picture of a large wind farm and asks: 'How do spinning blades generate electricity? What has to happen first?' Students predict and discuss, then the teacher tells them they will build a small working model of the same idea using paper.

Students open Textbook p. 123 and follow the step-by-step construction guide: draw two diagonals on a square sheet, cut halfway along each line, fold alternate corners to the centre, and pin to a stick. Each student builds their own pinwheel. Once built, students hold them near an open window or fan, or hold them up and walk quickly, observing the rotation.

Students record two observations in their notebooks: what makes the pinwheel spin, and how the rate of spin changes with more or less wind. The teacher connects this to how a real windmill's spinning blades drive a generator to produce electricity, and mentions that ancient Indian traders from Gujarat and Tamil Nadu used wind-powered sails for maritime trade long before electricity existed.
Students write one sentence connecting their pinwheel observation to the idea that moving air carries energy that can be put to use.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a physical model, test it under a natural force, and connect the model's behaviour to a real-world energy-conversion system.
periods.section_context: Paper pinwheel construction — diagonal cuts, folded corners, pin to stick; observation of spinning in wind; connection to windmills and electricity generation; ancient maritime wind-powered trade (Gujarat, Tamil Nadu).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'What would you change about your pinwheel to make it spin even faster?' to push students toward reasoning about blade angle or size. Encourage students to think about where in India wind farms might work best and why — connecting geography to energy resource use.

periods.activity_title: Sunlight in Focus and the Water Wheel — Solar and Water Energy
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Focus sunlight through a magnifying glass onto paper and observe what happens (p. 124)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagrams of magnifying glass setup and water wheel assembly (p. 124)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks two quick questions: 'Have you ever felt sunlight focus through glass and become very hot?' and 'Have you ever seen a wheel turned by water?' Students share brief experiences, setting the purpose: today they will experience both in a hands-on way.

Groups follow Textbook p. 124, Activity: magnifying glass focus. Each group holds the magnifying glass in direct sunlight or near a bright window and focuses the beam onto plain paper, observing what happens. They note how the concentrated spot differs from ordinary sunlight on paper. Safety reminder: do not look through the glass at the sun. Students record what they see.

Groups now build the water wheel following Textbook p. 124: make five holes around a paper cup, insert plastic spoons as blades, push a pencil through the base as an axle, and balance it on a container. They pour water gently onto the spoons and observe whether the cup rotates. Students record: does water make it move, and which direction does it turn? The teacher connects this to traditional gharaats — watermills in hilly areas that use flowing water to grind grain.

Students write a two-row comparison in their notebooks: Solar energy experiment — what happened and what form energy took; Water wheel — what happened and what form energy took. The connection to Cochin International Airport running entirely on solar energy is mentioned as a closing fact.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct two parallel investigations, record observations from each, and compare the energy sources and conversions involved.
periods.section_context: Magnifying glass focusing sunlight on paper — heat produced; paper cup water wheel with spoon blades — water flow causes rotation; solar energy; water energy; gharaats (traditional watermills in hilly areas); Cochin International Airport solar energy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Where in India would solar energy work best, and where would water energy work best — and why?' to connect the hands-on results to geography. If students are from hilly regions, invite them to share whether they have seen or heard of watermills or water-powered systems in their area.

periods.activity_title: Energy Flow Game — Linking Source, Type, and Use
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Energy Flow Game: match source, type, and use cards in groups and present to the class (p. 128)
materials: Pre-prepared paper slips — energy sources (Sun, wind, water, food, fuel, electricity), energy types (heat, light, movement, sound), uses (drying clothes, lighting a bulb, turning a turbine, cooking, running)
periods.visual_aids: Board list of energy sources, types, and uses as reference during discussion

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes one paper slip to each student without revealing what category it is. Students read their slip silently and think: is this a source, a type, or a use of energy? The teacher explains the task: each student must find the two others who complete their energy chain — source leads to type leads to use.

Students move around the room, reading each other's slips and negotiating matches following the structure in Textbook p. 128. Once a group of three is satisfied with their chain, they stand together and practise how they will present: 'Our source is ___; it produces ___ energy; which is used for ___.' Incomplete chains re-mix and try again.

Each group presents their chain to the class. The class votes on whether the chain is complete and correct. Where there is disagreement, a brief discussion clarifies — for example, the Sun can connect to heat (drying clothes) or to light (powering solar panels to light a bulb), showing that energy sources can serve multiple chains.

Students copy into their notebooks the energy chain their group formed, then write one additional chain of their own invention. The teacher closes by asking: 'Which sources in our chains are clean, and which produce pollution?' — linking the activity to the chapter's conservation theme.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify energy sources, forms, and uses and explain the chain of transformation from source to application.
periods.section_context: Energy Flow Game — paper slips for sources (Sun, wind, water, food, fuel, electricity), types (heat, light, movement, sound), uses (drying clothes, lighting a bulb, turning a turbine, cooking, running); source-to-type-to-use chains; clean versus polluting sources.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Can one source appear in more than one chain?' to push students beyond one-to-one matching toward understanding that energy sources are versatile. Allow students to invent new cards for local energy uses — a wood-fired chulha, a cycle dynamo, a water pump — to keep the game grounded in their own experience.

periods.activity_title: Clean Energy Home — Drawing a Plan for the Future
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw or make a simple plan of a clean energy home that uses solar, wind, or any such source of energy (p. 130)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the question from Textbook p. 130: 'Why is it better to use solar or wind energy instead of coal?' Students respond briefly in pairs, then a few share with the class. The teacher writes key reasons on the board: no pollution, renewable, freely available. Students then read the task for the period: design and draw a home that runs entirely on clean energy.

Students work individually to draw their clean energy home plan on drawing paper or a notebook page. They label each feature: where solar panels sit, where a small windmill might be placed, whether there is a water-heating panel, what devices inside the house run on which energy source. Students who finish quickly add a brief key or legend explaining their choices.

Students share their drawings in groups of three, explaining one feature they are most proud of and one question they still have about clean energy. Groups note any idea that appears in all three drawings — that shared idea is likely the most important feature of a clean energy home.
The teacher closes with the Textbook p. 130 prompt: 'What is the one thing you can do at home to save energy?' — each student writes one personal action they commit to, beneath their drawing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of clean energy sources by producing a labelled plan that shows how those sources would power a home.
periods.section_context: Clean energy home drawing — solar panels, wind energy, water heating; labelled features; reasons solar and wind are better than coal; personal energy-saving action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'What would your clean energy home look like if you lived in a hilly area instead of a city — or in a coastal area?' to prompt region-sensitive thinking. Encourage students whose families use solar water heaters or have experienced a wind turbine nearby to bring that knowledge into their plan.

periods.activity_title: My Energy Diary — Observing and Reflecting on a Day's Energy Use
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Make an energy diary for one day, recording every instance of electricity or fuel use (p. 130)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the reflection question from Textbook p. 130: 'What will happen if there is no electricity in your house for a day?' Students think silently for a moment, then share. The class lists on the board what they would lose — light, cooking, fans, entertainment, refrigeration — building a picture of how deeply energy is woven into daily life.

Students open Textbook p. 130 and begin constructing their energy diary for the current or most recent day at home. They recall and write down every instance they can remember of using electricity or fuel — from the morning light switched on to the last device used at night — in a simple three-column table: time of day / what they did / energy source used.

Students review their completed diary and respond to the two reflection items from Textbook p. 130: which two examples show energy being stored, and why is using clean energy better than coal. They annotate their diary entries with a small mark to show which could be replaced by a clean energy source and which could not.

Students write a short personal commitment — one sentence — on what they will change about their energy use, based on what they found in their diary. Two or three students share. The teacher closes by naming the chapter's core question: energy makes everything work, and the choices people make about energy shape the world around them — for better or worse.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically document their own energy use, identify opportunities for conservation, and articulate a personal action toward more responsible energy choices.
periods.section_context: Energy diary — recording electricity and fuel use across a day; instances of stored energy (battery, food, fuel); comparison of clean versus polluting energy sources; personal energy-saving commitment; impact of no electricity for a day.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask 'Were you surprised by how often you used energy without noticing?' to help students move from observation into genuine reflection. Treat the diary entries as private unless a student chooses to share — families have different resources and energy access, and the reflection should build awareness, not shame.

assessment_items.question_text: You look around a busy kitchen and notice: the gas flame is heating a pot, the fan is turning, the light is on, and the pressure cooker is making a sound. What is the one thing that ALL of these activities need in order to happen?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item checks whether students can identify energy as the common underlying cause of diverse kitchen phenomena, as developed in the opening discussion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify observable phenomena in everyday environments and connect each to a common underlying cause.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Water' suggests the student is thinking of cooking specifically (water boils, steam forms) rather than what is common to all the activities named — including the fan, light, and sound, none of which require water.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Electricity' reflects a partial understanding — electricity powers the fan and light, but not the gas flame or the pressure-cooker sound directly. The student has not generalised to the broader concept of energy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Air' may reflect the student associating the fan or the pressure-cooker sound with moving air, rather than identifying energy as the cause of all these changes.

assessment_items.question_text: A student blew up a balloon, held the mouth shut, and then let it go. The balloon shot across the room and made a loud noise as it deflated. What was stored inside the balloon before it was released, and what happened to that stored energy when the balloon was let go? Give two observations from the activity to support your answer.
expected_elements: Names the stored energy in the blown-up balloon (compressed air / stored energy from blowing).
States that the stored energy changed into movement (the balloon moved / flew across the room).
States that the stored energy also produced sound (the noise heard when the balloon deflated).
Provides at least two of the above observations as evidence.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate description of stored energy (compressed air, energy put in by blowing) converting to movement and sound. Both forms of energy output should be mentioned for full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple inquiry, record observations, and draw a conclusion about energy changing from one form to another.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Names stored energy in the balloon (compressed air or energy from blowing).
Identifies movement (kinetic energy) as one form the released energy took.
Identifies sound as a second form the released energy took.
Uses at least two observations from the activity as evidence for the conclusion.

assessment_items.question_text: When Meera plucked a thin rubber band stretched tightly over a box, she heard a high sound. When she plucked a thick rubber band with less tension, she heard a low sound. What does this tell us about the relationship between the rubber band and sound energy? Use the words 'mechanical energy' and 'vibration' in your answer.
expected_elements: States that plucking the rubber band is a form of mechanical energy (energy from movement or force).
Explains that the plucking causes the rubber band to vibrate.
Connects the vibration to sound energy being produced.
Notes that the type of sound (high or low) changes with the tension or thickness of the band, showing that more or less energy input changes the output.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit requires use of both 'mechanical energy' and 'vibration' in a meaningful way, not just insertion into the answer. Accept any equivalent description of energy transfer from finger to band to sound.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate through a hands-on investigation that mechanical action transfers energy and produces a detectable change in another form.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Identifies plucking as a mechanical action that puts energy into the rubber band.
Uses the word 'vibration' to describe what the rubber band does after being plucked.
Links vibration to the production of sound energy.
Connects changing tension or thickness to a change in the sound produced (demonstrating understanding of cause-effect in energy transfer).

assessment_items.question_text: In the diya activity, two diyas were set up: Diya 1 had a dry cotton wick and Diya 2 had a cotton wick soaked in oil. Both were lit at the same time. Diya 1 went out very quickly. Diya 2 kept burning for a long time. What does this tell us about oil?

options.label: A
options.text: Oil makes the wick catch fire more quickly than a dry wick.

options.label: B
options.text: Oil is a fuel that provides energy to keep the flame burning.

options.label: C
options.text: Oil cools the diya so the flame does not go out.

options.label: D
options.text: Oil is needed only to light the wick, not to keep it burning.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item assesses whether students can read the observation (Diya 2 lasted longer) and conclude that oil acts as fuel, consistent with the controlled comparison they made.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a controlled comparison, record what changes and what stays the same, and identify the factor responsible for the observed difference.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student noticed that Diya 2 lit well but confused 'igniting quickly' with 'burning longer' — they have not read the comparison accurately.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'oil cools the diya' indicates a misconception that oil has a cooling or protective function rather than an energy-releasing function — possibly confused with oil being used to reduce friction in other contexts.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option suggests the student believes oil is only a starter and the wick itself provides energy, missing the central lesson that the fuel is the energy source that sustains the flame.

assessment_items.question_text: In some villages in Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh, families keep their cattle on the ground floor of their home during cold winters, and the family lives on the floor above. A visitor asked: 'Why do people do this? It seems strange to keep animals inside.' How would you explain to the visitor why this is a sensible and clever way to use energy? In your answer, say what energy source is being used, how it works, and what it replaces.
look_for: Identifies the cattle's body heat as the energy source (animals release heat from the food they eat).
Explains that heat rises from the ground floor to the floor above, warming the family's living space.
States that this reduces or replaces the need for firewood, coal, or electricity for heating.
Connects the practice to the cold climate of mountain regions, showing awareness that geography shapes energy choices.
Uses reasoning rather than mere description — explains WHY it is clever, not just WHAT it is.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response will explain the mechanism (body heat rising), name what it replaces (firewood or electricity), and connect the practice to the cold mountain climate. Accept any well-reasoned equivalent. Regional variation note: students from Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, or Ladakh may draw on direct family knowledge — this enriches rather than changes the expected reasoning.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a natural energy source and a traditional cultural practice that harnesses it.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Names body heat of cattle as the energy source.
Explains that heat rises through the floor, warming the living space above.
States that this reduces dependence on firewood, coal, or electric heating.
Connects the practice to the cold climate of the mountain region (geography as context).
Provides evaluative reasoning — why this is clever or sensible — not just a description of what happens.

assessment_items.question_text: A student surveyed her classroom and found the following electrical devices: a ceiling fan, a tube light, a radio, and a laptop. She made a table showing what each device produces. Which row in her table is CORRECT?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The item checks whether students can accurately classify electrical devices by their primary energy output, as practised during the classroom survey activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe and classify devices in their environment by the type of energy output they produce.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Ceiling fan → Heat' suggests the student has confused the fan's primary output (movement/air circulation) with a heating device. They may be thinking of an electric heater.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'Tube light → Movement' suggests the student has not classified devices by their dominant observable output and may be confusing light with motion (perhaps thinking of a bulb's filament moving or flickering).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Laptop → Cooling' suggests the student has noticed that laptops sometimes feel warm or that cooling fans run inside them, confusing a by-product or component (cooling fan) with the device's primary energy output.

assessment_items.question_text: Arjun made a paper pinwheel and held it near an open window. The pinwheel began to spin. He then held it still and noticed it stopped. What energy made the pinwheel spin, and how does this connect to the way real windmills generate electricity? Write your answer in two or three sentences.
expected_elements: Names wind (moving air) as the energy source that made the pinwheel spin.
States that the moving air transfers energy to the blades, causing rotation.
Connects the pinwheel's spinning to real windmills, where rotating blades drive a generator to produce electricity.
Explains that when there is no wind, no energy is transferred and the pinwheel (or windmill) stops.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate explanation linking wind energy to rotation and rotation to electricity generation. Students are not required to use the word 'generator' if they can describe the concept clearly.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a physical model, test it under a natural force, and connect the model's behaviour to a real-world energy-conversion system.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Identifies wind (moving air) as the energy source for the pinwheel's rotation.
Explains that the wind transfers energy to the blades, making them spin.
Connects this to real windmills that use the same principle to generate electricity.
Notes that without wind, neither the pinwheel nor the windmill spins — showing understanding that the natural resource must be present for energy conversion to occur.

assessment_items.question_text: In one investigation, a student used a magnifying glass to focus sunlight on paper and noticed the paper became very hot. In a second investigation, she poured water onto a paper-cup water wheel and the wheel began to turn. What do these two investigations have in common? What is different about them? Write three sentences.
expected_elements: States what is common: both use a natural resource (sunlight and flowing water) to produce a useful energy effect — showing that natural resources can be converted into usable energy.
Identifies the difference: the sunlight investigation produced heat, while the water wheel investigation produced movement (mechanical energy).
Connects either or both to a real-world use: solar panels or solar heaters use concentrated sunlight; water wheels or turbines use flowing water to generate electricity or grind grain.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit if the student correctly identifies the common idea (natural resource converted to useful energy) and the different output forms (heat vs. movement). Accept reference to gharaats or Cochin Airport as real-world connections.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct two parallel investigations, record observations from each, and compare the energy sources and conversions involved.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Identifies the common idea: both investigations use a natural resource to produce a useful energy conversion.
States the difference in output: sunlight produced heat; flowing water produced movement (rotation).
Makes a real-world connection for at least one investigation (solar heater/panel for sunlight; watermill/turbine/gharaat for water wheel).

assessment_items.question_text: In the Energy Flow Game, a student received the card 'the Sun'. She needs to find two other students to complete her energy chain. One card must show a type of energy and the other must show a use. Which chain is CORRECT?

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun → Light → Turning a turbine

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item checks whether students can trace a complete and accurate source-type-use chain, as practised in the Energy Flow Game. Option D is partially correct (sunlight does produce light) but 'turning a turbine' is matched to water or wind, not direct sunlight in a home context — it represents a chain mismatch.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify energy sources, forms, and uses and explain the chain of transformation from source to application.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'The Sun → Sound → Running' shows a fundamental confusion about energy types — the student has not understood that the Sun produces heat and light, not sound, and that 'running' as a use requires food energy (from the body), not direct solar energy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'The Sun → Movement → Cooking' shows a partial chain error: the student associates the Sun with movement (perhaps thinking of solar-powered fans) but matches it incorrectly to cooking, which is a use of heat energy, not direct movement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'The Sun → Light → Turning a turbine' shows a plausible but mismatched chain: sunlight can produce electricity via solar panels (which could power a turbine), but 'turning a turbine' is most directly associated with wind or water energy chains, not direct sunlight. The student has conflated different chains.

assessment_items.task: Draw your 'Clean Energy Home'. Show at least two different clean energy sources in your drawing and label each one. Below your drawing, write one sentence explaining why you chose those energy sources and one sentence about what you personally can do to save energy.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: Where does the sunlight fall on your home? Where might wind blow? Is there a rooftop, a garden, or a yard? What devices inside the home need energy? Label each clean energy source and draw an arrow showing which part of the home it powers. Then write your two sentences below the drawing.
format_of_output: Labelled drawing showing at least two clean energy sources and the home features they power
One sentence explaining the choice of energy sources
One sentence stating a personal energy-saving action
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any home design that includes at least two correctly labelled clean energy sources (solar, wind, water, or others the student proposes) and that shows meaningful connections between source and use. The written sentences should reflect the student's own reasoning. Regional variation note: home designs will vary widely — rooftop solar suits urban homes, wind may be more relevant in coastal or hilly settings, small water channels in rural areas. All regionally appropriate designs are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of clean energy sources by producing a labelled plan that shows how those sources would power a home.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply their knowledge of clean energy sources to a design task, showing that they understand which sources are clean, how they can be used in a home context, and what choices support energy conservation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs attention to the physical features of the home (rooftop, garden, yard) and asks students to connect each energy source to a specific use — this ensures the drawing is conceptually grounded, not decorative. The two written sentences move from design reasoning to personal action.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response labels at least two different clean energy sources, shows arrows or annotations connecting source to use, and writes sentences that demonstrate understanding of why those sources are preferable. A weak response shows a drawing without labels, lists clean energy sources without connecting them to the home's design, or writes generic sentences not grounded in the drawing.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their home plan in words with a rough sketch. Students who do not have access to coloured pencils may use a single pencil with labelled annotations. The key observable outcome is the reasoning behind the choices, not the artistic quality of the drawing.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled drawing with two written sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing format allows students to spatialise their understanding of energy flow — showing which part of the home each source powers — while the written sentences require them to move from design to reasoning and personal commitment, both of which are observable and assessable by the teacher.

assessment_items.task:
Think about one day at home. Fill in the table below with at least five entries, then answer the two questions that follow.

Table:
| Time of day | What I did | Energy source used |
|-------------|-----------|-------------------|
| | | |

Question 1: Look at your table. Which of the energy sources you listed are clean, and which produce pollution? Circle or mark them.
Question 2: Choose one activity from your table and describe what you could do differently to use less energy or a cleaner source.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start with the very first thing that happened in the morning — was a light switched on? Was food cooked? Did someone use a vehicle? Work through the day in order. For each activity, ask: what energy was needed for this to happen, and where did that energy come from?
format_of_output: Completed table with at least five entries (time, activity, energy source)
Marked or annotated table distinguishing clean from polluting sources
One written response identifying a change the student could make to reduce or clean up their energy use
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any five or more realistic daily activities with their energy sources correctly identified. The marking of clean versus polluting sources should be consistent with the chapter's content (coal, wood, petrol, diesel = polluting; solar, wind, water = clean; gas and electricity may be discussed as better or worse depending on their origin). The student's proposed change should be specific and realistic. Regional variation note: energy sources will differ significantly across households — some cook on wood, others on LPG or electricity; some travel by bus, others walk. All regionally accurate entries are correct and should be affirmed.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically document their own energy use, identify opportunities for conservation, and articulate a personal action toward more responsible energy choices.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the chapter's framework of energy sources and their consequences to their own life, distinguish clean from polluting sources in a real context, and propose a meaningful conservation action — demonstrating that the chapter's values have been internalised.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students through their day chronologically, reducing the cognitive load of remembering and ensuring that entries are spread across morning, afternoon, and evening activities. The two follow-up questions push from documentation (what I did) to evaluation (what I could do differently).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response has specific, varied entries (not just 'used electricity' repeatedly), correctly identifies the energy source for each, marks clean and polluting sources accurately, and proposes a change that is genuinely feasible for that student's household. A weak response lists vague activities, fails to identify the energy source for most entries, or proposes a change that is not connected to anything in their table.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who do not have electricity at home will have equally valid (and often richer) tables showing reliance on firewood, kerosene, or sunlight — these are not deficient responses. Students with limited literacy may complete the table with drawings and labels. The teacher may allow verbal responses for the written questions for students who need it.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Completed data table with annotations and written response
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table format mirrors systematic data collection — a core inquiry skill — while the written questions require the student to analyse and act on their collected data. This mirrors the real-world practice of an energy audit, making the task meaningful beyond the classroom.
